claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite with tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix.
Adding 2–3 wt% Ag to the powder blend before spark plasma sintering will produce Ag-enriched layers at W–Cu interfaces.
The Ag-enriched interfacial layers will be ultrathin, continuous, and coherently bonded.
SPS at 1050–1100 °C under an inert atmosphere with controlled cooling will permit limited Ag diffusion and formation of the proposed coherent interphase.
High-temperature atomic diffusion can control the formation and composition of layered interfacial structures in metal-matrix composites.
SPS can produce a thin, chemically or metallurgically bonded multilayer interface in a composite.
Silver has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Silver is metallurgically compatible with both tungsten and copper.
Silver will preferentially segregate to W–Cu interfaces during sintering.
The Ag-rich interphase will reduce thermal boundary resistance at W–Cu interfaces.
The Ag-rich interphase will act as a conduction bridge that improves electron and phonon transport across W–Cu interfaces.
Reducing W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance will increase the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
Adding only 2–3 wt% Ag will leave the bulk microstructure substantially intact.
Adding only 2–3 wt% Ag will preserve the irradiation-resistant properties associated with tungsten.
The Ag-modified composite may exhibit a 20–30% increase in effective thermal conductivity relative to an otherwise comparable Ag-free W–Cu composite.
The Ag-modified composite will retain mechanical strength and durability comparable to the Ag-free control.
The Ag-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the Ag-free control under relevant service conditions.
Higher Ag additions, processing outside 1050–1100 °C, or alternative processing methods may fail to produce the desired interface and property improvements.
